title: Units, dimensions and estimation
note: Every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions, so checking units catches many errors. Convert by multiplying by ratios equal to 1. Report results with sensible significant figures, and estimate first so you can tell when an answer is absurd.

read.title: A spacecraft lost to units
text: In September 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter fired its engine to enter orbit and was never heard from again. Investigators found that one team's software reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds, while the navigation software expected newton seconds. Each small error was off by a factor of about 4.45, and over months of flight the trajectory drifted until the craft passed far too close to Mars.

The lesson is not that one unit system is better. It is that units carry meaning, and every number that crosses an interface must state its units. Engineers protect themselves with dimensional analysis: every term in a correct equation must have the same dimensions. If you add a force to a pressure, something is wrong.
A second habit is estimation. Before calculating, guess the order of magnitude from simple assumptions. If a hand-held drill seems to need a megawatt, the arithmetic or the model has failed.

Finally, results should not claim more precision than the data support. A load known to two significant figures cannot produce a stress known to six. Writing 8.6 rather than 8.6154 tells the reader honestly what you know.

q.q: What caused the Mars Climate Orbiter loss?
